definition.rule: A beastman chieftain with one or more warbands may establish a beastman clanhold by securing land and capturing or constructing a stronghold.
Beastman clanholds are managed as domains with the special rules below.

classification.rule: Population density is limited because beastmen rely on simple horticulture, local pastoralism, and foraging rather than intensive agriculture.

families.rule: Each clanhold family consists of 1 beastman warrior and 1 or more noncombatants.
Noncombatants can include females, whelps, elderly, and slaves.
The specific beastman race must be recorded because it affects availability of tribal warriors.
Ogre and troll families count as 4 families each for population limits and growth.

growth.condition: The chieftain actively raids at least once per month.
growth.rule: The clanhold gains additional monthly population growth based on current number of families.
Use the ACKS p. 129 population growth table, treating the clanhold as 2 population categories smaller than an equivalent human domain.

settlements.limit: Urban population must remain below 250 urban families.
Urban investment cannot increase settlement size or market class.
Urban families can never exceed 12.5% of the clanhold's peasant population.

military.rule: Clanhold chieftains cannot conscript peasants or levy militia.
Clanhold chieftains may levy up to 1 tribal warrior per family.
Clanhold chieftains may hire other beastmen in the area as mercenaries.
Clanhold chieftains may employ human and demi-human mercenaries only if they are chaotic.

realm_management.rule: A chieftain may establish a realm by founding additional clanholds and assigning them to henchmen, typically sub-chieftains, or by conquering and annexing an existing domain.
Human and demi-human domains under beastman rule reduce base morale by 2, in addition to any alignment penalty.

vassalage_limits.limit: Chieftains cannot offer charters of monopoly.
Chieftains cannot offer grants of title.
vassalage_limits.rule: When calling to arms, a chieftain may call half of available tribal warriors as 1 favor, or all available tribal warriors as 2 favors.

definition.rule: A chaotic domain is a clanhold ruled by a chaotic human, demi-human, or sapient monster of high intelligence, or managed as a vassal domain within the realm of such a ruler.

establishment.rule: A chaotic adventurer may establish a chaotic domain instead of the normal domain for class and race.
establishment.condition: The decision is made when the domain is secured.
establishment.step: Instead of clearing beastmen from the area, recruit a clanhold chieftain as a henchman.
If the current chieftain is unsuitable, replace him with a more pliable sub-chieftain.
Once the clanhold chieftain is brought into service, the adventurer becomes a chaotic domain ruler.

followers.condition: An adventurer of 9th level or higher establishes a chaotic domain.
followers.rule: The ruler attracts followers and families in the usual numbers.
These followers and families are beastmen instead of humans or demi-humans.
The beastmen are of the same race as the clanhold.

exceptions_from_clanholds.rule: Chaotic domains may be civilized only if within 25 miles of a city or large town in the same realm.
Chaotic domains may be borderlands only if within 50 miles of civilized areas in the same realm.
Once population exceeds 125 peasant families per 6-mile hex, excess peasant families provide only half normal land revenue.
Urban settlements are not limited to 250 families or 12.5% of peasant population.
Urban settlements may be increased in size or market class.
Value of investment in chaotic domains is halved.
It costs 2,000gp to attract 1d10 new families.
It costs 50,000gp to achieve market class V.
Urban revenue remains 7gp per family regardless of settlement population.

definition.rule: A ruler with an existing realm of any type may annex a clanhold to that realm.
A realm with at least one chaotic domain is a chaotic realm.

rules.rule: Chaotic realm rulers may hire beastmen as mercenaries.
Chaotic realm rulers may employ human and demi-human mercenaries only if they are neutral or chaotic.
Lawful domain rulers become vassals of a chaotic realm ruler only if conquered and annexed.
Domains ruled by lawful vassals in a chaotic realm suffer a -2 morale penalty for alignment difference.

section.name: beastmen_as_slave_labor
section.rule: Using beastmen as slave labor does not make a domain a chaotic domain.
All normal slave labor rules from ACKS pp. 250-251 apply.

definition.rule: A typical clanhold for each beastman race is equivalent to a typical wilderness lair of that race.
Ogre and troll families count as 4 families for population limits and take up 4 times the land area.

village_rules.rule: Peasant families may live in centralized clusters and still remain peasant families.
A clustered set of peasant homesteads does not count as an urban settlement unless it has urban families.
An urban settlement is distinct mechanically because it creates a Class VI market, equipment for purchase, and/or specialists.
Beastman wilderness "villages" should be treated as clustered peasant homesteads representing typical clanholds, not urban settlements.

definition.rule: Use this table to build beastman realms in wilderness regions.
For each terrain type, the first row gives average clanholds per 24-mile hex and chance of a clanhold per 6-mile hex.
Remaining rows give the 1d100 result ranges for each clanhold's race.

procedure.step: Determine the number of clanholds for the terrain.
Roll 1d100 for each clanhold to determine race from the terrain column.
Treat each result as either a wilderness lair or an average clanhold from the demographics table.
Place clanholds in a logical settlement pattern within the 24-mile hex.
Organize the clanholds into one or more realms at the Judge's discretion.

definition.rule: Use this table to build diverse wilderness domains and realms, determine what beastman families arrive when a clanhold or chaotic domain grows, or benchmark availability of beastman mercenaries.
The first row gives average beastman families per terrain type, listed as families per 24-mile hex / families per 6-mile hex.
Remaining rows give 1d100 result ranges for the race of each family, with raw percentages in parentheses.

adjustment_option.rule: Judges who want sparser wilderness may reduce the suggested number of clanholds and families.

definition.rule: In tribal cultures, all able-bodied men, and some women, serve as warriors.
A leader of a tribal domain may levy tribal warriors into an army.
Tribal domains include beastman clanholds and chaotic domains.

levy_rules.rule: Up to 1 tribal warrior per tribal family may be levied without reducing domain morale or domain revenue.
Any additional levies are treated as militia.
The levy may occur all at once or over time.
If the number of tribal families changes, the number of available tribal warriors changes accordingly.
If population is reduced, some tribal warriors must be released to return to their villages.
If population increases, new tribal warriors become available.
Tribal warrior casualties can only be replaced through population growth.

service_rules.rule: When recruited, tribal warriors arrive trained and equipped according to tribal custom.
The troop mix levied per 120 tribal warriors is determined by the tribal warrior troop type table.
The Judge may create additional troop type tables for specialized nations or races.
While serving, tribal warriors must be paid wages appropriate to troop type, using Mercenary GP Wage per Month from Domains at War: Campaigns.

base_rules.rule: Tribal warriors use the base morale of their troop type.
Tribal warriors levied from domains with Steadfast or Stalwart domain morale gain a one-time +1 morale increase.
Tribal warriors levied from domains with Apathetic or Demoralized domain morale suffer a one-time -1 morale decrease.
Tribal warriors may gain other morale modifiers from working conditions, as mercenaries do.

morale_and_loyalty_triggers.rule: Tribal warriors make morale rolls in battle when casualties exceed their army's break point.
Tribal warriors make loyalty rolls whenever they suffer a calamity.
Usual calamities include routing from battle, suffering 25% or more casualties, being out of supply, or going without pay for a month.
Tribal warriors also make morale rolls after 3 consecutive months of service without receiving spoils from a battle or siege equal to at least their wages.

departure_rules.rule: When a loyalty roll is required, use the Unit Loyalty table.
Tribal warriors who leave service return to their villages if possible.
If return is not possible, they become brigands or mercenaries.

references.reference: ACKS p. 129 population growth table for additional clanhold growth.
Domains at War: Campaigns domain militia, annexation, mercenary wages, and unit loyalty subsystems.

confidence_notes.note: The source OCR is degraded in several tables. I normalized obviously blank cells to none where the distribution pattern strongly suggests no entry, especially: woods/lizardman in clan distribution; jungle/hobgoblin and jungle/kobold in clan distribution; desert/troglodyte in clan distribution; barren/troglodyte in family distribution.
The hills and mountains hobgoblin entries in the clan distribution table are printed as 0 rather than a dash. I preserved the printed 0 rather than converting it.
The tribal warrior troop table headers were normalized from OCR-corrupted labels to jutland, iv_kingdom, skysos, and hobgoblin.
The lizardman horse_archers entry in the tribal warrior troop table is printed as a double dash. I treated it as none.
The Unit Loyalty table reference is unresolved in the source, which prints p. XX rather than a final page number.
